title: Lord, have mercy
hookLine: three short Greek cries left inside the Latin Mass

cards: For many centuries, the Mass in the West was said in Latin. The readings, the prayers, the priest's words over the bread.
But near the start, right after the confession, the choir or the people would sing three short cries in a completely different language. Not Latin. Greek.
It's like finding one line of an old family song, in grandma's language, still sung in the middle of a house where nobody speaks it anymore. It was never put into Latin.

teach.b: Kyrie eleison. Lord, have mercy. Christe eleison.
Christ, have mercy. Kyrie eleison. Lord, have mercy.
Kyrios is Greek for Lord, a title the New Testament gives Jesus. Eleison means have mercy.

teach.h: KEPT IN GREEK INSIDE THE LATIN.
teach.b: The cry came into the Roman Mass from the Greek-speaking churches of the East, and when the West prayed in Latin, this piece was kept in its original tongue, like a stitch that holds the two halves of the Church together.
For centuries each cry was repeated three times, nine in all. Now it's usually twice each, six in all, and often said or sung in English. And this cry isn't a church invention.
It's the cry of desperate people on the road in the Gospels. Two blind men sitting by the road hear Jesus passing, and shout: have mercy on us.
A mother from outside Israel, whose daughter is suffering, follows him shouting, in the Douay-Rheims: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou son of David." People who had run out of every other option.
So the Kyrie at Mass is the whole church standing in their place on the roadside. Dictionaries trace one more thing in the word.
The Greek for mercy, eleos, gave a word for giving to the poor, eleēmosynē. That word traveled through Latin into Old English and shrank, over centuries, into our word alms.

teach.h: HAVE MERCY ON ME, O LORD, THOU SON OF DAVID.
teach.b: Mercy that you ask for, and mercy that you give, come from the same root.

how: Near the start of Mass, after the penitential act (or as part of it), the Kyrie is said or sung, usually twice for each line: Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy, in English or in the original Greek.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: mercy, and the root of alms

s: the Kyrie is in Latin, like the rest of the old Mass
it's Greek, kept untranslated inside the Latin Mass.
the English word alms comes from the Greek word for mercy
eleos gave eleēmosynē, giving to the poor, which shrank over centuries into alms.
the Kyrie was invented as a church formula
it echoes cries from the Gospels: blind men and a desperate mother shouting have mercy.

games.q: you're a mother from outside Israel, and your daughter is suffering. Jesus is walking past. what do you do?
o: wait quietly for a better moment.
send someone else to ask for you.
games.why: she followed him, crying out: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou son of David." the Kyrie at Mass stands in her place on the road.

practice: Breathe in slowly, and on the out-breath, if you pray, say quietly: Kyrie eleison; then Christe eleison on the next, and Kyrie eleison on the third.
If you don't pray, you can simply let three slow breaths go, thinking of someone, maybe yourself, who could use mercy today. Then let the quiet stay.
